analysis.one_liner: Bans federal officials and their families from owning or trading individual stocks while in office.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in any of the six committees it was sent to, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred Members of Congress, senior federal officials, judges, the President, and the Vice President, along with their spouses and dependent children, from owning or trading individual stocks, commodities, futures, and similar investments, with violators docked a full month's salary for every month of violation. It would also have eliminated nearly all outside earned income for Members of Congress and made the post-employment lobbying ban for former Members permanent rather than the current two years for senators and one year for House members. The bill never moved past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, who would gain a rule that lawmakers and senior officials cannot hold or trade securities that could benefit from their official decisions. Federal officials themselves would be pushed into diversified funds, Treasury bonds, and government retirement plans, which the bill expressly allows.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans concerned about official conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: It would ban Members of Congress, their spouses and dependents, the President, the Vice President, political appointees, judicial officers, and senior congressional staff from owning or trading securities, commodities, futures, and derivatives, while permitting diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasury securities [S2] [S3].
Violating officials would forfeit their full monthly salary for each month of violation, and names of violators would be published on a public ethics office website [S2] [S3].

It would ban all outside earned income for Members of Congress (capping preserved exceptions like medical practice and compensated teaching), and make the post-employment lobbying ban for former Members permanent instead of the current two-year ban for senators and one-year ban for House members [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, senior officials, and their families, who would have to divest individual stock holdings within 90 days; and former Members and lobbying firms, who would lose the revolving door that now lets ex-lawmakers lobby their former colleagues after one or two years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and future lobbyists among them

drawbacks.text: A blanket ban would bar officials from even modest individual investments, which critics argue could deter people of ordinary means from running for office and push Members toward blind trusts or divestment at awkward times [S3].
A lifetime lobbying ban goes far beyond current law and beyond what many reform proposals offer, and could be challenged as overbroad restriction on former officials' ability to earn a living [S3].

The bill assigned enforcement to the existing House and Senate Ethics Committees, which are run by Members themselves, so its penalty structure would depend on the same people it regulates choosing to enforce it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core stock-ownership ban is a straightforward conflict-of-interest rule with real teeth (a month's salary per month of violation). The harsher edges — a full outside-income ban and a lifetime lobbying ban — go beyond the middle-ground versions of this idea that have drawn broader support, and enforcement would still rest with Member-run ethics committees. As written, the benefits to public trust would likely outweigh the costs, but the bill never got far enough for that trade-off to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees and two subcommittees, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Andy Kim introduced the bill on February 25, 2022, and it was referred to the Judiciary, Financial Services, Agriculture, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Ways and Means Committees [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors during its ten months in the House [S4] [S5].

The only further action was two subcommittee referrals — to the Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit Subcommittee in March 2022 and the Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet Subcommittee in November 2022 — with no hearings, markups, or votes ever scheduled [S5].
It died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without any chamber voting on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and other covered federal officials keep the ability to hold and trade individual stocks and keep the current short cooling-off periods before lobbying. Anyone who profits from the revolving door of former Members joining lobbying firms is also better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who kept stock-trading rights

for.name: Rep. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the six committees of referral (including Judiciary)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and with zero cosponsors from either party there is no roll-call record of where members stood.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and covered federal officials
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stocks and forgo nearly all outside income, with a month's salary forfeited for each month of violation. Because Members control the House and Senate agenda, the bill's fate rested with the group it would have regulated.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and the revolving door
industries.note: The bill would make the post-employment lobbying ban for former Members permanent, cutting off a pipeline in which ex-lawmakers lobby their former colleagues after only one or two years out of office.

industries.industry: Brokerage and asset management firms serving wealthy officials
industries.note: Trading and holdings by covered officials would be banned outright, and compliance would route officials toward diversified funds and Treasury securities rather than active brokerage accounts.
